cells.tense: You are here, with the pen, and the adjusting is steady.
cells.ask: Name the one thing you'd keep tending even if it stopped giving back, and keep tending it this week because you chose it.
cells.core:
You're the one holding the middle of this, and the middle moves. When something you're growing needs more — more water, more patience, more room — you feel it before it shows, and you give it. You're not managing growth like a project. You're reading it while it changes, and that's why what you tend tends to come through.

The same hand that adjusts is free to feed something it hasn't picked yet. You can add one thing to what you're feeding, not because it's asking, but because you are. What you have isn't a method you invented. It's attention that stays fluent, and it's free to turn slightly — to look at what's next without dropping what's in front of you. That turn is the growth. Say out loud what you're keeping, and keep saying it while you work.
cells.sheetLine: You adjust what's growing because you're reading it, not managing it.
cells.verb: Adjusting continuously — sensing when to add, subtract, or blend
cells.place: In the care for what is growing

cells.tense: You are bracing for a harmony that hasn't arrived, and you're living there.
cells.ask: Let one honest distinction stand without smoothing it over — say the true thing once and leave the room without fixing it.
cells.core:
You're running ahead of the thing you're tending. Somewhere forward is a place where nothing is unsettled, and you're already living there — so you adjust before anyone has said what they need. You smooth a difference before it can become a real one.

That smoothing is what it costs. The thing you're growing needs edges, and you're sanding them down before they set. The sharpness is still there — it's just pointed at keeping the peace instead of keeping the growth. What would it be like to let one true thing hold? To say it once, clearly, without turning it into a problem to be solved? Your care doesn't get tested if every hard edge is softened first. Set it down once, and see what the thing does when it has to stand on its own shape.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping the temperature steady at the cost of the true temperature.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you a long time ago.
cells.ask: Sit with one other person — no agenda, no fixing — and let them see you without making yourself useful.
cells.core:
The center you work from isn't where you left it. You're scattered across the rooms you're caring for, and every engagement pulls you a little further out, so the sense of when to add and when to hold back is running thin. You keep showing up for what's growing, but you're not really in the room while you do it.

It isn't that you've stopped being able to tune. It's that the tuning needs somewhere to draw from. What's gone quiet isn't effort or more care. It's being met — the kind of contact where you don't have to be useful for someone to stay. That's what pulls the center back. Don't push yourself to feel more into the thin place. Let someone else be with you there first, without you handing them anything you're tending, and see if the tuning comes back on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You've been everywhere for what's growing and nowhere for yourself.

cells.tense: You are already writing the way this grows, with the pen down.
cells.ask: Point to one thing you've carried from someone else and say out loud that you chose to keep it.
cells.core:
You're already shaping what's coming up around you — in the timing you give things, the way you listen, what you let pass and what you quietly hold. But it gets described as if the growing were doing that on its own. The hand that adjusts is still moving. Nobody has put your name on it.

Somewhere in there is what you were handed and chose to keep — the way you were taught to tend, the thing someone showed you that you took on. That's not less yours for having come from somewhere. It's how any of it works. Say out loud one thing you kept on purpose, and the pen is back in your hand. Not as a new method you invented, but as a line you're carrying forward because you decided to.
cells.sheetLine: You're already shaping it. You just haven't said so.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person keeps a steady hand on how things grow — the record shows the capacity is present and adjusting, not that it is currently being held well everywhere. A reader could reasonably say they are not the one deciding what to pass on, or that the harmony is not theirs to keep. The ask survives being wrong because it offers a concrete move the person can test without needing the read to be confirmed, and the cell itself can be refused with the person still ahead. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that flatters the steadiness instead of showing what the steadiness is for.
